reason: A capsule can have a stalk (pedicel). The French example is about the pedicel itself, but the English ones are correct.
Lobes can point upward (ascending). I could not check what the FLOPO part class is, because its name is blank.
Leaf blades can be sticky (glutinous).
A blade can be solid, as opposed to hollow. There is only one example.
A bulb can be large.
Lenticels can be large. The bare example 'enlarged' is uncertain.
Buds can be sessile (without a stalk).
Inflorescences can be flexible. 'On lengths of flex' is a stray example.
A perianth or its lobes can be bent back (reflexed). Some examples are really about the lobes.
Sepals or sepal horns can be terete (round in cross-section).
Roots can radiate from a point. This describes how they are arranged, but the pair is meaningful.
The part name is blank and the examples mention both base and apex. A rule would need to know which anatomy class this is and whether 'flared' applies to it.
Bracteoles can be scaly, in the sense of scale-like.
'Coarse teeth' means large or stout teeth, not a rough surface. The PATO term is read wrongly.
Berries can be fleshy or juicy.
Racemes can be branched or unbranched.
An exocarp can be inconspicuous. The examples are partly about cells, but the pair is fine.
Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be lance-ovate.
The part name is blank. 'Urceolate' and 'pouched' are different shapes, and 'concave 3-D shape' is too vague for them. A rule would need to map urceolate and pouched to specific terms.
'Ellipsoid' is not 'prolate'. The ellipsoid term should be used instead.
A length-to-width ratio is a real measure of a perigynium.
Achenes can be symmetric or asymmetric.
Teeth can be cartilaginous (firm and gristle-like).
A perigynium can be present or absent. The 'numerous' examples are really counts, so those are less certain.
'Texture' is only the general attribute. A rule would need to map words like scabrous and scabrid to specific value terms and not use the attribute alone.
The examples show a beak (or similar part) that can be smooth.
Anthers can have stripes or bands.
'Angled' means having angles or ridges, not bent. The PATO term is read wrongly.
This is only the general texture attribute. The examples (resinous, fibrous) need specific value terms, so a rule must separate them.
Auricles can be spiny or spinulose.
Lobes can be thread-like (filiform).
Involucral bracts or their tips can be straight.
Bracts can be dull or shiny.
Glochids can be inconspicuous.
A mentum can be present or absent.
The part can have ear-like lobes (auricles). The examples mix the quality with the presence of auricles.
Branches can be suppressed or undeveloped.
Styles can bear bristles.
Leaf sinuses can be deep.
Thorns and prickles can point backward (retrorse).
A perianth can be narrow. Some examples are about the tube or wings, which are parts of the perianth.
The examples count flowers per corymb, not corymbs. The counted thing is a different part, so the pair is a wrong reading.
Hydathodes can be sunken.
Cauline leaves can be present or absent. One example is unrelated.
Tepals can have a notched tip (emarginate).
Areoles can be subcircular.
'Characteristic' is a vague root term. The examples are specific qualities (glabrous, smooth) that need their own terms.
Bracts can have an entire (smooth, unbroken) margin.
An apex or lip can be truncate (cut off square).
A seed coat can have wavy margins or cell walls.
Sori can be globose.
Sori can be straight or curved.
Leaf blades can be cylindrical.
A gynoecium or pistil can be slender. One example is about a stipe.
The examples describe seed pits or epidermal cells, not the seed. The hexagonal quality belongs to the cell or pit, so the part is wrong.
A fruit surface can be sculpted. One example is about the endocarp.
Inflorescences such as spikes can be laterally compressed.
The part can be short. Some examples compare it with another organ, which is an extra relation.
Stipules, including the ocrea, can be loose.
The examples count cones per node, not nodes. The counted part is the cone, so the pair is a wrong reading.
